c.tagline: Guatemala's highland second city, a colonial center for Spanish schools and volcano treks

taxi.fareNote: Taxis lack meters, so agree on a fare before departure; tuk-tuks (mototaxis) are the cheapest way to cover short distances around town

emergency.note: 110 reaches the National Civil Police (PNC), 123 reaches Bomberos Voluntarios for fire and ambulance; response outside the center can be slow

avoid.reason: Avoid the Minerva bus terminal/market fringes and outlying zones after dark, when street robberies occur.
Watch for pickpockets at La Democracia and Minerva markets, take radio taxis at night, and hike nearby volcanoes only with a group or guide due to trail robberies.

hood_desc: The neoclassical heart of Xela, centered on the grand Parque Centro América and its columned Passage. Cafés, language schools, and the cathedral cluster within a few blocks here.
A semi-rural district on the city's edge that serves as the main gateway for hikes up Santa María and Santiaguito volcanoes. Quiet and sparsely built up.
A hillside residential area prized for panoramic views over the valley, popular with longer-term language-school students renting rooms with local families.
A mixed residential and commercial zone housing the Teatro Municipal and several markets, offering a more local, less touristed slice of the city.

water.note: Drink bottled, filtered or boiled water only.

transit.pay: Cash only, paid to driver or fare collector
transit.map: No official transit map; routes are learned locally or via word of mouth
transit.note: No metro or formal rail; the walkable center covers most needs, with tuk-tuks and minibuses for outlying areas

air: La Aurora International Airport (GUA), main gateway
train: No passenger rail service in Guatemala
bus: Extensive Pullman and 'chicken bus' network to Guatemala City (~4 hrs) and surrounding highland towns

tip.r: Around 10% at sit-down restaurants is customary; small change for tuk-tuk or taxi drivers is welcomed but not required

food.name: Caldo de Res
food.desc: Clear beef-and-bone broth loaded with corn on the cob, carrot, chayote and potato, eaten with rice, lime and tortillas - Xela's cold-highlands staple.

places.name: 7 Caldos Xela
places.note: Whole menu built on Guatemalan broths; the beef caldo comes in a huge bowl with all the trimmings.

places.name: El Recreo
places.note: Local favourite for regional plates, singled out by diners for its caldo de res and churrasco.

places.name: Mercado La Democracia comedores
places.note: Market cook-stalls serve caldo de res at midday for a fraction of restaurant prices.

food.name: Paches
food.desc: Thursday-only tamales made from mashed potato instead of corn, filled with pork or chicken in red recado and steamed in banana leaf.

places.name: Mercado La Democracia
places.note: Thursday paches vendors line the market; the classic Xela way to eat them, hot from the pot.

places.name: Mercado Central
places.note: Central-market stalls sell paches and tamales in the late afternoon and evening.

places.name: Utz Hua
places.note: Small typical-Guatemalan restaurant near the centre that cooks paches and other regional tamales.

food.name: Pepian
food.desc: Guatemala's national stew: chicken or beef in a dark sauce of toasted seeds, chillies and tomato, thickened to a rich gravy and served with rice.

places.name: La Flauteria
places.note: Small bistro repeatedly recommended for its pepian de pollo and other typical plates.

places.name: Restaurante Bonifaz
places.note: Xela's long-established hotel dining room, a formal setting for classic Guatemalan pepian.

places.name: Utz Hua
places.note: Typical-food kitchen doing pepian, jocon and kaqik at everyday local prices.

food.name: Chuchitos
food.desc: Fist-sized corn tamalitos with a nub of meat and tomato recado, wrapped in corn husk and topped with dry cheese - the everyday Guatemalan snack.

places.name: Mercado La Democracia
places.note: Baskets of hot chuchitos sold from doorways and stalls all afternoon.

places.name: Parque Centro America evening vendors
places.note: Street sellers work the main plaza at dusk with chuchitos, atol and tostadas.

places.name: Mercado Minerva
places.note: Xela's biggest market; chuchito vendors work the food aisles from early morning.

food.name: Shecas
food.desc: Quetzaltenango's own bread - a dense, faintly sweet spiced roll of wheat and rye flour, eaten with coffee or split around beans and cheese.

places.name: Xelapan
places.note: Xela-founded bakery chain; the easiest reliable place to buy shecas fresh all day.

places.name: Mercado La Democracia bread stalls
places.note: Bread sellers stack shecas by the basket, still warm, at the market's edge.

places.name: Cafe El Cuartito
places.note: Popular central cafe where shecas and local pastries come alongside highland coffee.

food.name: Hilachas
food.desc: Shredded beef slow-cooked in a tomato and chilli sauce with potato and carrot - a homely Guatemalan Sunday dish found on every comedor menu.

places.name: El Mirador Restaurante
places.note: Neighbourhood restaurant serving hilachas and other home-style Guatemalan plates with a city view.

places.name: 7 Caldos Xela
places.note: Rounds out its broth menu with hilachas and other traditional stews.

places.name: Mercado Central comedores
places.note: Cheap market kitchens run hilachas as a daily special with rice and tortillas.

food.name: Atol
food.desc: Hot corn-based drink poured from cauldrons - atol de elote sweet with fresh maize, atol blanco with beans and chilli, or shuco, its darker cousin.

places.name: Parque Centro America atol carts
places.note: Evening vendors ladle atol de elote and shuco into cups on the main plaza.

places.name: Mercado La Democracia
places.note: Market atoleras have been pouring atol from morning pots for generations.

places.name: Mercado Minerva
places.note: Atol stalls near the bus terminal serve travellers from dawn.

food.name: Quetzalteca
food.desc: The aguardiente named for the city itself - a clear cane spirit, now also bottled in tamarind, rose of Jamaica and coconut flavours.

places.name: Casa Babylon
places.note: Long-running traveller bar in the centre where Quetzalteca shots and cocktails are standard.

places.name: Tertulianos
places.note: Central bar-restaurant popular with locals and students for evening drinks.

places.name: Mercado La Democracia liquor stalls
places.note: Buy the flavoured bottles cheaply where Xela residents actually buy theirs.

landmarks: Parque Centro América
The elegant neoclassical heart of Xela, a grand plaza of columns and monuments ringed by the cathedral, banks and municipal palace.
Catedral del Espíritu Santo
The city's cathedral pairs a lavish 1535 colonial facade, preserved freestanding, with the modern basilica rebuilt behind it after earthquakes.
Pasaje Enríquez
A once-grand 1900s Parisian-style shopping arcade off the plaza, now Xela's favourite nightlife corner of bars, murals and live music.
Teatro Municipal
A stately neoclassical theatre inaugurated in 1895, symbol of Quetzaltenango's coffee-boom golden age and still hosting concerts and festivals.
Templo a Minerva
A curious Greek-style temple built in 1917 to honour education under dictator Estrada Cabrera, standing beside the city's bustling terminal market.
Cerro El Baúl
A forested hill park above town with lookout points over the valley, picnic spots and a famous giant concrete slide.
Fuentes Georginas
Steaming volcanic hot-spring pools wrapped in cloud-forest ferns on the slopes of Volcán Zunil, the region's most beloved half-day escape.
Volcán Santa María
A near-perfect 3,772-metre cone towering over Xela, whose strenuous pre-dawn ascent rewards climbers with views of erupting Santiaguito below.
Iglesia de San Andrés Xecul
A day-trip village church with an exuberant canary-yellow facade swarming with saints, angels and jaguars, among Guatemala's most photographed.
Laguna Chicabal
A sacred crater lake ringed by cloud forest where Maya altars line the shore, reached by a misty hike from San Martín Sacatepéquez.

train.note: There is no passenger rail in Guatemala; FEGUA's regular services ended in 1996 and heritage steam charters stopped in 2007. Quetzaltenango's own Ferrocarril de Los Altos, the country's only electric railway, opened in 1930, was wrecked by mudslides and demolished in 1933, and survives only as a small museum in the city. The nearest active project is the proposed Metro Riel in Guatemala City.

intl.to: San Cristobal de las Casas & Comitan (Mexico) - tourist shuttle via the La Mesilla border
Tapachula (Mexico) - via the Tecun Uman / El Carmen crossing
intl.op: Transportes Galgos Inter and Linea Dorada - tickets at their Zona 3 offices

intl.to: San Salvador (El Salvador), Tegucigalpa (Honduras) & Managua (Nicaragua) - board in Guatemala City, about 4 hrs from Xela

bus.note: Chicken buses and second-class services use the sprawling Terminal Minerva on the northwestern edge of town, about 3 km from the Parque Centro America, while the first-class companies - Galgos, Linea Dorada, Alamo and Transportes Fortaleza - run from their own offices in Zona 3 near the Rotonda. Guatemala City is 4-4.5 hrs away on the CA-1 Pan-American Highway, Panajachel about 2.5 hrs and Antigua about 4 hrs by direct tourist shuttle. Most tickets are still bought at the counter in cash; shuttles, including the long day-run to San Cristobal de las Casas via La Mesilla (10-12 hrs with the border stop), can be booked online through GuateGo (https://guatego.com/). Border formalities at La Mesilla and Tecun Uman are straightforward for most nationalities but slow, so allow an hour.

ferry.note: Quetzaltenango sits at about 2,330 m in the western highlands with no navigable water anywhere near it, so there is no ferry of any kind; the nearest boats are the Lake Atitlan lanchas at Panajachel, roughly 2.5 hrs away by road.

half.name: Zunil
half.blurb: A small town about 20 minutes south sits beside hot springs and is known for its market and the cult shrine of Maximón.

half.name: Almolonga
half.blurb: A farming town roughly 10 minutes from Xela grows vegetables in volcanic soil and holds a busy Saturday produce market.

half.name: San Francisco El Alto
half.blurb: A hilltop town about 25 minutes away hosts one of Central America's largest weekly markets every Friday, selling livestock, textiles, and produce.

full.name: Chichicastenango
full.blurb: A highland town about two hours away holds a famous market where Maya vendors sell textiles, pottery, and incense outside a colonial church.

full.name: Lake Atitlán
full.blurb: A volcanic lake ringed by Maya villages lies roughly two and a half hours away, reached by a winding mountain road.
